Hal Lindsey, The 1980s: Countdown to Armageddon (1980), suggested the decade could be the last.
The 1993 Midwest flood was one of the costliest in American history, yet history continued.

Futurists respond that Jesus told believers to watch the signs, so it is natural to relate news to prophecy. Many admit sensational books do harm, but they say careful observation of trends is still biblical watchfulness.
Does 2 Timothy 3:1-5 describe the world just before a future rapture?
On the fulfilled reading, Paul described Timothy's own day. He told Timothy to "turn away" from such people and said their folly would soon be plain to all.

Read in context, Paul's "last days" in 2 Timothy 3 are the days Timothy lived in. Paul lists lovers of self, lovers of money, boasters and people with a form of godliness. Then he tells Timothy, "From such people turn away" (3:5). That command only makes sense if Timothy would meet them. Paul says they "creep into households" in the present tense (3:6). He compares them to Jannes and Jambres who opposed Moses. He also says they "will not make further progress, for their folly will be plain to all" (3:9). That is hopeful, not gloomy. Hebrews 1:2 calls the time of Christ "these last days". So the passage warns about false teachers in the last days of the old covenant age.
1 Timothy 1:20 names Hymenaeus and Alexander, false teachers Timothy actually faced.
2 Timothy 2:17-18 names Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said the resurrection had already happened.

Many futurists read 2 Timothy 3 as a description of the final decline of society before Christ returns. Amillennial and many evangelical scholars say "last days" covers the whole church age, so the passage fits Timothy's time and every later time.
What is the main reason for endless speculation about the end?
Prophecies that were already fulfilled are treated as still future. Then they are applied to whatever is happening in the news.

The fulfilled reading names one root error above all others: reading fulfilled prophecy as unfulfilled. Whether the "end" means the rapture, the millennium or the new heavens and new earth, speculation grows when texts are removed from their time. Many prophecies concerned the coming of the Messiah, the judgment on the old covenant order, and the end of the temple. These events happened in the first century. When readers push them into the future, they must find new events to match. So each generation finds a new Antichrist, a new Babylon and a new set of signs. The way out is to ask what the prophecy meant to the people who first received it, and whether Scripture or history records its fulfilment.
Luke 24:44: Jesus said everything written about him in the Law, Prophets and Psalms must be fulfilled.
The Roman destruction of the temple in AD 70 ended the sacrifices Daniel 9:27 speaks of.

Futurists answer that the opposite error is also real: treating unfulfilled prophecy as fulfilled, as Hymenaeus did with the resurrection (2 Timothy 2:18). They argue many prophecies, like the visible return and resurrection, clearly remain future.
How is reading fulfilled prophecy as future like waiting for a Messiah who has already come?
Many in the first century did not see Jesus as the fulfilment of the prophets, so they kept waiting. Christians do something similar when they push fulfilled prophecies into the future.

The fulfilled reading offers a respectful comparison. John says Jesus came to his own, and many of his own did not receive him. Some Jewish leaders did not see that the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms spoke of him. So they kept waiting for the Messiah's first coming. Many Jewish people today, for sincere reasons, still wait. Christians believe the messianic promises were fulfilled in Jesus' birth, death and resurrection. The point is not to blame anyone. The point is a warning about method. Christians can make the same kind of mistake with prophecies about the judgment of AD 70. When fulfilled words are projected into the future, they are then forced onto current events, and confusion follows.
Acts 13:27: those in Jerusalem did not recognise Jesus yet fulfilled the prophets by condemning him.
Many Jewish believers, like the apostles and thousands at Pentecost, did receive Jesus (Acts 2:41).

Futurists reject the comparison, saying they fully accept Christ's first coming and simply await the second. Many Christians also stress Romans 11 and expect a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ. All agree such comparisons must avoid blame on Jewish people.
Why must we pay close attention to the time words in prophecy?
Time words like "near", "soon", "this generation" and "about to" fix when an event happens. If they are ignored, a prophecy can be made to fit any age.

On the fulfilled reading, the first rule in reading prophecy is to notice the time indicators. If you miss when an event is said to happen, you will misjudge what it means. The New Testament says the end of all things was at hand for Peter's readers. Revelation says its events were near. Jesus says "this generation" and "some standing here". These phrases are as much a part of the text as the images. A comparison helps. If a letter says, "I will visit you soon," no reader thinks it means two thousand years. The writers chose words of nearness on purpose. Respecting those words is part of taking the Bible literally and seriously.
Habakkuk 2:3 says the vision "will not delay"; it was fulfilled in Babylon's fall in 539 BC.
Daniel was told his vision was for a distant time (Daniel 8:26), showing God uses different time words for far events.

Futurists say time words must be read alongside God's view of time (2 Peter 3:8) and the possibility of delay. Many evangelicals accept the near words as near for some events (AD 70) but not for the final return.
When were the "last days" according to Hebrews 1:1-2?
Hebrews says God spoke "in these last days" through his Son. The last days began with Christ's first coming and closed the old covenant age.

On the fulfilled reading, Hebrews puts the last days in the first century. God spoke long ago through prophets in many ways. Now, "in these last days", he has spoken by his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). The writer and his readers were living in those days. Hebrews later says Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin (9:26). The "last days" are therefore the last days of the old covenant age, the era of the fathers and the prophets. That era ended when the temple and its sacrifices were removed in AD 70. Peter said the same at Pentecost: the outpouring of the Spirit was what Joel said would happen "in the last days" (Acts 2:16-17).
Acts 2:16-17: Peter says, "This is what was spoken by the prophet Joel."
The letter to the Hebrews was written while temple sacrifices still continued (Hebrews 10:1-2).

Amillennialists and most evangelicals agree the last days began with Christ but say they continue until his return. Dispensationalists often distinguish the "last days" of Israel from the last days of the church. Full preterists say all last-days language ended in AD 70.
What does Hebrews 8:13 mean when it says the old covenant was "ready to vanish"?
The writer says the first covenant was growing old and was near to disappearing. On the fulfilled reading, it vanished in practice when the temple fell in AD 70.

Read covenantally, Hebrews 8:13 is a time text. God made the first covenant obsolete by announcing a new one through Jeremiah. The writer adds that what is growing old is "near to vanishing away". The Greek word for "near" (engus) is the same word used for the kingdom being "near" and the summer being "near". The old system was still standing when Hebrews was written: priests still offered sacrifices daily (10:11). But its end was close. Within a few years Roman armies burned the temple. No sacrifice has been offered there since. The new covenant is better because Jesus' blood is better than the blood of animals, and because God now speaks through his Son.
The last daily sacrifice ceased in July AD 70 during the siege (Josephus, Jewish War 6.2.1).
Jeremiah 31:31-34 is quoted in full in Hebrews 8:8-12.

Most Christians agree that the old covenant was fulfilled in Christ. Some say it was made obsolete at the cross, not in AD 70, and that "near to vanish" simply describes its fading. Dispensationalists often expect a future temple, but not as a means of salvation.
How did the coming of Christ in the flesh show that the last days had begun?
Under the old covenant no one could see God's face and live. In Jesus, God took on flesh and was seen, heard and touched.

On the fulfilled reading, the incarnation itself proves that the last days had arrived. God told Moses, "You cannot see my face, for no one may see me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Before Christ, God spoke through dreams, prophets, written words and types. In the last days he spoke in his Son. John says the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we saw his glory. In his letter, John writes of what "we have seen with our eyes" and "our hands have touched". This is a new way of revelation. The proof that the last days had come was that God had spoken in a Son. The final stage of revelation had begun in the first century.
John 1:18: no one has ever seen God; the only Son has made him known.
Exodus 33:18-23: Moses saw only the "back" of God's glory.

All Christian views agree that the incarnation is God's final revelation. They differ on when the last days end: in AD 70 (preterists), at Christ's return (amillennial and postmillennial views), or with a future seven-year period (dispensationalists).
What do 1 Peter 1:20, Acts 2:17 and 1 John 2:18 say about when the "last times" were?
Peter says Christ appeared "in these last times" for his readers. Peter applies Joel's "last days" to Pentecost. John says, "It is the last hour."

On the fulfilled reading, three apostles speak with one voice. Peter writes that Christ was chosen before creation but "was revealed in these last times for your sake" (1 Peter 1:20). The readers lived in the last times. At Pentecost, Peter said the gift of the Spirit fulfilled Joel's prophecy about "the last days" (Acts 2:17). John told his readers that many antichrists had come, "so we know that it is the last hour" (1 John 2:18). John even gives evidence: the antichrists proved it. The theologian Gordon Clark observed that "the last days" in these texts clearly means the time of Peter himself. So the New Testament places the last days in the apostolic generation.
Gordon H. Clark, II Peter: A Short Commentary (1975), comments that the last days meant Peter's own time.
1 John 2:19: the antichrists "went out from us", meaning they were known church members.

Amillennial and many evangelical interpreters agree that the last days began in the first century, but they say this period stretches until Christ's return. Futurists often stress a final, intense "last days" period still ahead.
What did Jesus mean when he said the disciples would not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes?
On the fulfilled reading, Jesus spoke of a coming in judgment within the disciples' mission to Israel. That points to AD 70, not to a far-off return.

In Matthew 10, Jesus sends the twelve to the lost sheep of Israel. He warns of persecution and says, "When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. You will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes" (10:23). The audience is the twelve. The place is Israel. The time is the span of their mission. So the coming of the Son of Man must fall within their lifetimes. The fulfilled reading sees this as Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem and its leaders. The same phrase "Son of Man comes" appears in Daniel 7:13, where it describes a coming to God to receive a kingdom, not a coming to earth.
Acts 8:1-4 shows believers fleeing from city to city as Jesus foretold.
Daniel 7:13-14: the son of man comes "with the clouds" to the Ancient of Days.

Interpretations vary widely: some say the coming is the resurrection or Pentecost; some futurists say the mission to Israel will resume in a future tribulation; Albert Schweitzer argued Jesus expected the end at once and was mistaken.
Why did Jesus tell the high priest that he would see the Son of Man coming on the clouds?
Jesus said to Caiaphas and the council, "You will see." On the fulfilled reading, they saw Christ's rule shown in the judgment of AD 70.

At his trial, Jesus told the high priest, "From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven" (Matthew 26:64). He used "you", plural, to speak to the council. He joined Psalms 110:1 with Daniel 7:13. "From now on" points to something beginning soon. Read covenantally, the leaders "saw" Christ's enthronement in the resurrection, the spread of the gospel, and finally in the fall of their city and temple. In the Old Testament, God "rides on a swift cloud" when he comes in judgment on Egypt. The cloud-coming is a picture of divine judgment and rule, not only a future bodily descent.
Isaiah 19:1: the Lord rides a swift cloud and comes to Egypt in judgment.
Ananus son of Annas, of Caiaphas's own priestly family, was killed in Jerusalem during the war in AD 68 (Josephus, Jewish War 4.5.2).

Futurists say "you will see" means the council will see Christ at the final judgment, after resurrection. Some scholars say Jesus spoke of his vindication and exaltation, which they would "see" through events after the resurrection.
What did Jesus mean by "if I want him to remain until I come"?
Jesus hinted that John might live until his coming. John did outlive Jerusalem's fall, while Peter died before it.

After telling Peter how he would die, Jesus answered Peter's question about John: "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" (John 21:22). John adds that a rumour spread that he would not die, but Jesus had not said that. He had only spoken of John remaining until he came. On the fulfilled reading, this fits Matthew 16:28 exactly. Some would live to see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. Peter was martyred in Rome around AD 64-67. John, by early tradition, lived until the time of Trajan, well past AD 70. So one disciple saw the coming in judgment and others did not. The text expects a coming within a lifetime.
Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3.4) says John lived until the time of Trajan (from AD 98).
Peter's death is traditionally dated in Nero's persecution after the fire of Rome in AD 64.

Many interpreters say Jesus was speaking hypothetically, to rebuke Peter's curiosity, and made no promise about John. Some link "until I come" to the visions John received in Revelation, while others see the final return in view.
What did Paul mean by "salvation is nearer", "the day is at hand" and "the Lord is near"?
Paul told the Romans and Philippians that the day was close for them. He also said God would "soon" crush Satan under their feet.

On the fulfilled reading, Paul's time words apply to his readers. He told the Romans to wake up because "salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed" (13:11). "The night is far gone; the day is at hand" (13:12). He promised that "the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet" (16:20). To the Philippians he wrote, "The Lord is near" (4:5). The word "soon" (en tachei) is the same phrase that opens Revelation. Paul linked these words to present duties: put off darkness, live honourably, be gentle. On this reading, the "day" was the coming judgment that would end the old order and free the young church from its chief persecutors.
Romans 16:20 echoes Genesis 3:15, the promise that the serpent's head would be crushed.
Much early persecution of Christians came from synagogue authorities in Judea and the diaspora (Acts 13:50; 14:19).

Many scholars say Paul's nearness language refers to the next great event in God's plan, Christ's return, which could come at any time. Some critical scholars say Paul expected Christ's return in his lifetime and was wrong.
What did Paul mean by "the present distress" and "the time is short" in 1 Corinthians 7?
Paul told the Corinthians that a time of distress was upon them and that the "form of this world" was passing away. He gave practical advice for that crisis.

Read in context, Paul gives advice about marriage "in view of the present distress" (1 Corinthians 7:26). He says "the time has been shortened" (7:29) and "the present form of this world is passing away" (7:31). These are not general remarks for all ages. Paul ties them to a crisis that was "present" for his readers. That is why he advised the unmarried to stay as they were, while saying marriage was no sin. On the fulfilled reading, the "world" passing away was the old covenant order, which ended within about fifteen years. Jesus had already warned, "Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days" (Matthew 24:19). The coming upheaval made family life hard.
Paul wrote 1 Corinthians about AD 54-55, roughly fifteen years before the fall of Jerusalem.
Famine and unrest in the empire in the 50s may also lie behind "the present distress".

Some scholars think the "present distress" was a local famine or persecution in Corinth. Others think Paul expected Christ's return soon. Most agree his advice was shaped by a specific crisis and was not a ban on marriage.
What did Paul and Hebrews mean by the "ends of the ages" and the "consummation of the ages"?
Paul said the ends of the ages had come upon his readers. Hebrews says Christ appeared at the consummation of the ages to put away sin. The ages were ending then.

On the fulfilled reading, the New Testament places the end of the ages in the first century. Paul writes that Israel's history was recorded "for our instruction, on whom the ends of the ages have come" (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says that Christ "has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself" (9:26). The disciples had asked about "the end of the age" (Matthew 24:3). These texts do not speak of the end of the planet. They speak of the close of an era: the age of the law, the temple and the old covenant. The new covenant age, which has no end, had dawned.
Isaiah 9:7: of the increase of the Messiah's government there will be no end.
Ephesians 3:21 speaks of glory to God "to all generations, forever and ever", showing the new age continues.
Amillennialists say the "end of the ages" began with Christ but will be completed at his return. Futurists often read "the end of the age" in Matthew 24:3 as the end of the present church age.
What did James mean by "the coming of the Lord is near" and "the judge is standing at the door"?
James wrote to Jewish believers suffering under rich oppressors. He told them to be patient because the Lord's coming was near and the judge was at the door.

On the fulfilled reading, James gives a clear time text. He writes to the twelve tribes in the dispersion (1:1). He warns rich landowners who withheld wages and killed the righteous: "Weep and howl for the miseries that are coming" (5:1). Then he tells believers, "Be patient until the coming of the Lord" (5:7) and "the coming of the Lord is near" (5:8). He adds, "The judge is standing at the door" (5:9). A judge at the door is about to enter. James wrote before AD 70, probably in the 40s or 50s. The judgment on the land and its oppressive leaders came in the Jewish war. The farmer's patience for the early and late rains fits a short wait.
James, the brother of Jesus, was killed in Jerusalem in AD 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1).
Matthew 24:33 uses the same image: "he is near, at the very gates."

Most commentators say James uses "near" to urge readiness for Christ's final return, which could come at any time. Some critical scholars hold James expected a return in his lifetime that did not occur.
Why did Revelation say its events "must shortly take place" and told John not to seal the book?
Revelation opens and closes with nearness: "shortly", "the time is near", "I am coming quickly". Daniel sealed his book because it was far off; John did not.

On the fulfilled reading, Revelation brackets its visions with time words. It shows "things which must shortly take place" (1:1). "The time is near" (1:3). The same phrases return at the close (22:6, 10). Jesus says, "I am coming quickly" (22:7, 12, 20). The contrast with Daniel is striking. Daniel was told to seal up his vision because it referred to "many days" in the future (Daniel 8:26; 12:4). Daniel's time span was about four centuries. John is told the opposite: do not seal the book, for the time is near. If four centuries was "far", two thousand years cannot be "near". So most of Revelation's judgments must have fallen soon after it was written.
Daniel 8:26 sealed a vision fulfilled under Antiochus IV in 167 BC, about four centuries later.
Revelation 3:11 tells the church at Philadelphia, "I am coming quickly; hold fast."

Futurists say "shortly" (en tachei) can mean "swiftly" when it happens, and "near" is from God's point of view (2 Peter 3:8). Idealists say the events are always near because the conflict runs through history. Historicists see the book unfolding from the first century on.
Does "the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world" in Revelation 3:10 mean the whole planet?
The word is oikoumene, "the inhabited world", often meaning the Roman Empire. The hour was "about to come" and was promised to a real church in Philadelphia.

On the fulfilled reading, Revelation 3:10 is a local promise with a near time. Jesus tells the church in Philadelphia that he will keep them "from the hour of trial that is about to come upon the whole world". The Greek word for "world" here is oikoumene. Luke uses it when Caesar Augustus ordered a census of "all the world", meaning the Roman Empire (Luke 2:1). The word "about to" (mello) signals nearness. The trial would test "those who dwell on the earth" or "land". The promise only comforts the Philadelphians if the trial came in their lifetime. The years AD 64-70, with Nero's persecution, civil war in Rome and the Jewish war, fit this hour.
Luke 2:1: Augustus taxed "all the world" (oikoumene), meaning his empire.
In AD 68-69 Rome had four emperors in one year, a crisis felt across the empire.

Pre-tribulation futurists say Revelation 3:10 promises the church removal from a future worldwide tribulation. Others say "keep from" means protection through it. Idealists apply it to trials in every age.
What does "in a very little while, he who is coming will come and will not delay" mean in Hebrews 10:37?
Hebrews quotes Isaiah and Habakkuk to tell suffering believers that the wait would be very short. "A little while" in the New Testament means within the hearers' lifetime.

On the fulfilled reading, Hebrews 10:37 is one of the strongest time texts. The writer urges believers not to throw away their confidence. He adds, "For yet a very little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay." He blends Isaiah 26:20 and Habakkuk 2:3. Elsewhere in the New Testament, "a little while" means a short time within the hearers' life. Jesus said, "Yet a little while I am with you" (John 7:33). He said, "A little while, and you will not see me" (John 16:16). James says life is a vapour that appears "for a little while" (4:14). In the same chapter Hebrews says believers "see the day approaching" (10:25). The writer expected the coming within his readers' days.
John 16:16-19: "a little while" was the days between Jesus' death and resurrection.
Habakkuk 2:3 promised Babylon's judgment would "not delay"; Babylon fell in 539 BC.
Futurists say the writer stresses certainty and readiness, and that God's "little while" may be long by human standards. Some see a near fulfilment in AD 70 and a final one at Christ's return.
What is the doctrine of "imminency", and do the time texts support it?
Imminency says Christ's return could happen at any moment but may not be soon. The fulfilled reading says the texts do not say "may" or "could"; they say "near" and "soon".

Dispensational writers define imminency this way: an important event is likely to happen, could happen soon, and may take place at any time, though not necessarily very soon. The fulfilled reading asks where the texts use such words of possibility. Revelation says "must shortly take place". James says "is near". Peter says "is at hand". Hebrews says "will not delay". These are statements, not possibilities. If the apostles had wanted to say "perhaps soon", Greek had words to do so. Reading words in their plain, normal sense is the stated goal of literal interpretation. On that rule, the time texts say a great event would happen within the first readers' lives.
Jesus could speak of a long delay when he meant one: "after a long time the master returned" (Matthew 25:19).
Revelation 1:1 uses dei, "must", a word of certainty, not chance.

Dispensationalists hold that imminency protects watchfulness: since no sign must come first, believers must always be ready (Titus 2:13). Post-tribulation futurists reject any-moment imminency but still see Christ's return as future.
Why are the time texts the most important element in Bible prophecy?
They anchor prophecy to real history. If they can be stretched or ignored, the Bible can be made to mean anything, and a Bible that means anything means nothing.

On the fulfilled reading, the time texts are the key that unlocks the rest. Images in prophecy, like sun, moon, stars, beasts and clouds, are often symbolic. Readers can disagree about them. But words like "this generation", "near" and "about to" are plain words. They tell us when to look. If we fix the time first, the meaning of the images becomes clearer. If we ignore the time, the images can be applied to any nation, leader or disaster. That is why prophecy charts change every decade. Sound interpretation lets the clearest parts explain the harder parts. The time words are among the clearest parts.
Many prophecy charts from the 1970s that named the Soviet Union, the Common Market of ten nations, and 1988 have since been withdrawn.
Matthew 24:34 sets the time frame for the images in Matthew 24:29-31.

Futurists say the content of a prophecy, such as worldwide events and a visible return, also limits its timing, and that time words must be read in harmony with it. Most interpreters agree time words matter but weigh them differently.
Why do grammar and historical setting decide when a prophecy is fulfilled?
Without the setting, a passage can be made to fit any generation. The time Jesus gave is part of the meaning, not a detail to be set aside.

On the fulfilled reading, almost any meaning can be read into a verse if its grammar and history are ignored. Jesus spoke to particular people, in a particular place, about particular events. When he said "you", "this generation" or "some standing here", those words set limits. If the time is missed, the Olivet Discourse can be applied to the fourteenth century, to 1948 or to the next war. That creates endless confusion. The chief problem for those who place Matthew 24-25 in our future is that they must set aside these limits. Sound interpretation asks first: who was speaking, to whom, when, and about what? Only then do we apply the passage to our own lives.
Nehemiah 8:8: the Levites read the law and "gave the sense", helping people understand it.
Matthew 24:1-3 sets the scene: the disciples are looking at the temple buildings when they ask their question.

Interpreters of every view affirm grammatical-historical reading. Futurists argue that the same method shows some events, like a worldwide visible return, could not have happened in AD 70. The debate is about which details carry the most weight.
What did Jesus promise in Matthew 16:27-28?
He said the Son of Man would come in his Father's glory with his angels to repay each person. Some standing there would not die before seeing him come in his kingdom.

On the fulfilled reading, Matthew 16:27-28 joins a great coming to a short time limit. Verse 27 describes the Son of Man coming "in the glory of his Father with his angels" to "repay each person according to what he has done". Verse 28 begins "Truly I say to you" and says that "some of those standing here will not taste death" before they see this. "Some" implies that most would die, but a few would still be alive. So the event had to be far enough away that most hearers would be dead, yet near enough that some would live to see it. A coming two thousand years later does not fit. A coming one week later does not fit either.
"Taste death" is a Hebrew way of saying "die" (compare Hebrews 2:9).
Of the twelve, tradition says only John lived long after AD 70.

Many futurists say verse 27 is the second coming but verse 28 is a different event, often the transfiguration. Some amillennialists see the resurrection and Pentecost as the kingdom "coming with power". Critical scholars say Jesus expected the end soon and was wrong.
Was the transfiguration the fulfilment of Matthew 16:28?
On the fulfilled reading, no. The transfiguration came six days later, when all the disciples were still alive. "Some will not taste death" would then mean almost nothing.

Many link Matthew 16:28 to the transfiguration because it follows in the next verses (17:1-8). But the fulfilled reading sees a problem. Jesus said some standing there would not die before they saw the event. That wording implies that most of them would die first. The transfiguration took place "after six days". If it were the fulfilment, Jesus would be saying that most of his hearers would die within a week. Also, verse 27 speaks of coming with angels to repay each person for their deeds. No judgment or reward took place on the mountain. The transfiguration was a glimpse of Christ's glory, and Peter later remembered it that way. It was a preview, not the fulfilment.
2 Peter 1:16-18: Peter recalls the transfiguration as seeing Christ's majesty.
Henry Hammond (1653) argued the transfiguration cannot fulfil the verse because no reward to each person occurred.
